subsection: 3. Partition and Northern Ireland under the Unionist Party, 1912–1949

notes.b: Partition was the product of unionist resistance to Home Rule, British attempts to find a settlement, and the 1918 election result. The Government of Ireland Act 1920 gave effect to it.
points: Unionists were a clear majority in the six north-eastern counties of Antrim, Armagh, Down, Fermanagh, Londonderry and Tyrone, but not in the wider province of Ulster, which had nationalist majorities in Donegal, Cavan and Monaghan.
Unionist leaders from 1912 demanded the exclusion of the six counties from any Home Rule settlement, and the Ulster Volunteers made this demand a threat of force.
Lloyd George's 1916 attempt at a settlement proposed temporary exclusion of the six counties; it collapsed because nationalists and unionists disagreed on whether exclusion would be permanent.
The 1918 election confirmed a territorial split: Sinn Féin won most seats in the south and west, while unionists held most of the north-east seats.
The Government of Ireland Act 1920 created two Home Rule parliaments: one for Northern Ireland, covering the six counties, and one for Southern Ireland, covering the other twenty-six.
The Northern Ireland parliament opened in Belfast on 22 June 1921, when King George V addressed it.
The Anglo-Irish Treaty of December 1921 allowed Northern Ireland to opt out of the Irish Free State, and it did so in December 1922, which left the border in place.

The Boundary Commission, provided for in the Treaty, was meant to adjust the border; it reported in 1925 and its findings were kept secret, and the border was confirmed by the Tripartite Agreement of 3 December 1925.

notes.h: Violence and security in the north, 1920–1922
notes.b: The creation of Northern Ireland was accompanied by sectarian violence in Belfast and the building of a security system that relied on part-time unionist forces.
points: Catholic workers were expelled from Belfast shipyards in July 1920, the first major sectarian expulsions after the Government of Ireland Act.
Violence between Catholic and Protestant communities in Belfast from 1920 to 1922 killed several hundred people and drove many families from their homes.
The Ulster Special Constabulary was formed in 1920, with A, B and C divisions; the part-time B Specials were drawn largely from the Protestant community.
The Royal Irish Constabulary was replaced by the Royal Ulster Constabulary in 1922, a force that was largely Protestant in composition.

The Special Powers Act (Northern Ireland) of 1922 gave the government powers of internment, detention without trial, curfews and the banning of organisations, and it was renewed by the Stormont parliament.

notes.h: The Unionist government and its institutions, 1921–1940
notes.b: The Ulster Unionist Party controlled Stormont almost without interruption. It shaped the electoral system and local government to protect its majority.
points: James Craig led the Northern Ireland government as Prime Minister from 1921 until his death in 1940.
Nationalist members initially refused to take their seats at Stormont, leaving the Unionist Party to govern without effective opposition.
Proportional representation was abolished for local government elections in 1922, and for Stormont elections in 1929, when a first-past-the-post system was introduced.

Derry's corporation remained under unionist control in the 1920s and 1930s, although the city had a nationalist majority, through ward boundaries and a franchise that favoured property owners; this is the most cited example of gerrymandering.
The Stormont parliament building was opened in 1932 on a hill outside Belfast, a permanent symbol of the Northern Ireland state.
The Unionist Party's dominance rested on the exclusion of most Catholics from power in local councils and the civil service, as well as on its control of electoral rules.

notes.h: Discrimination in housing, jobs and policing
notes.b: Catholics made up about a third of the population of Northern Ireland and were the main target of discrimination in the state's institutions.
points: Catholics were about a third of Northern Ireland's population, and most of the nationalist community in the north lived in Belfast, Derry and the border counties.
Local councils allocated public housing by ward and points systems that favoured Protestant families, leaving many Catholic families in overcrowded and substandard accommodation.
Employment in the shipyards, the public service and the Special Constabulary was dominated by Protestants, and many Catholics were excluded from skilled and public-sector jobs.
The B Specials were used as a reserve police force, and their composition was an important cause of nationalist grievance about security.
Nationalists saw the Special Powers Act as the state's instrument against their community, and internment and detention were used most against republicans.

notes.h: The economic and social effects of partition
notes.b: Partition divided an integrated economy and left Northern Ireland dependent on heavy industry in a time of depression.
points: The border created a customs and trade frontier across an island whose industries and markets had been integrated, cutting the north-east's links with southern markets.
Belfast's shipbuilding industry, centred on Harland and Wolff, declined sharply in the inter-war years, and the linen industry faced falling demand.
Unemployment in Northern Ireland was high through the 1920s and 1930s, and it was worst in the shipyards and linen mills.
The Outdoor Relief riots in Belfast in 1932 were protests by unemployed men and women against cuts in relief payments.
In the Free State, partition cut off the Belfast market and the northern ports, and the Free State's economy depended on Britain's market for its agriculture.
Northern nationalists had no representation in the government of the Free State and were not able to shape policy at Stormont, leaving them politically isolated.

notes.b: Craig was the leading unionist figure in the Ulster crisis and the first Prime Minister of Northern Ireland. He is judged as a strong leader who secured the state, and as a figure whose rhetoric deepened sectarian division.
points: Craig (1871–1940) was a Belfast stockbroker and a Unionist MP at Westminster, a close ally of Edward Carson from 1912.
He organised the Ulster Volunteer Force's arms imports and was a leading figure in the Ulster Unionist Council's resistance to Home Rule.
He served as Civil Lord of the Admiralty in the British government until 1921 and then became Prime Minister of Northern Ireland, a post he held until 1940.
He was made Viscount Craigavon in 1927, and his government built the Stormont system, using the Special Powers Act and the B Specials.
In a 1934 speech he described Northern Ireland as a ‘Protestant parliament and a Protestant state’; the phrase is the most quoted example of his sectarian rhetoric.
Contemporary unionists saw him as the man who had secured the state, while nationalists regarded him as the architect of a sectarian system.
Historians such as Patrick Buckland, in his histories of unionism, emphasise his leadership of a state that protected the Protestant majority, while others stress his pragmatism in government.

notes.b: Bates was the Minister for Home Affairs for most of the inter-war period and controlled policing, local government and electoral law. He is most associated with the security system and the abolition of proportional representation.
points: Richard Dawson Bates was a unionist politician and a leading member of the Ulster Unionist Party in Northern Ireland.
He was Minister for Home Affairs from 1921 for more than two decades, responsible for the police, the Special Powers Act and local government.
He oversaw the Royal Ulster Constabulary and the B Specials, and supported the internment and detention of republicans under the Special Powers Act.
He piloted the 1929 electoral reform that abolished proportional representation for Stormont elections.
Nationalists regarded him as the chief architect of discrimination in policing and local government, and his name became a byword for the Stormont security system.
Historians stress his role in the structures of Unionist control, although they note that his legislation shaped Northern Ireland's politics for decades.

notes.h: Assessment: the Unionist state's achievements and limits
notes.b: Judgements on the Unionist government depend on whether it is measured by stability and security or by its treatment of the nationalist minority and its economic performance.
points: Achievements: the Unionist government created a stable parliamentary system, kept Northern Ireland within the United Kingdom, and survived the violence of 1920–22 and the Depression.
Limits: the state excluded its Catholic minority from power in local government and many public jobs, and it relied on coercive powers that were used against nationalists.
Contemporary unionists judged the state as a successful bulwark against a united Ireland under Catholic rule; nationalists judged it as a state of discrimination.
Later historians emphasise that the Unionist Party's dominance rested on electoral engineering and communal fears, and they debate how far the state could have been reformed.
Partition's economic costs fell most heavily on the working class of Belfast and on the border counties, and the government's response to 1930s unemployment was limited.

keyTerms.definition: The division of Ireland in 1920–21 into Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland, which left the six north-eastern counties in the United Kingdom.
The political movement that opposed Home Rule and sought to keep the north-east of Ireland in the United Kingdom.
The unequal treatment of Catholics in housing, jobs, policing and local government in Northern Ireland, which nationalists saw as the core of the Unionist state.
The Act that created separate parliaments for Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland, the legal basis for partition.
The 1922 Northern Ireland law giving the authorities powers of internment, detention and curfew, used against republicans and nationalists.
The body provided for in the Treaty to adjust the Irish border, which reported in 1925 but left the border unchanged.
The drawing of electoral boundaries to give one party an unfair advantage, used by unionists in Derry's local government.
The seat of the Northern Ireland parliament outside Belfast, opened in 1932 as a permanent symbol of the state.
The part-time security force formed in 1920, whose B Specials were largely Protestant and used against nationalists.
An electoral system in which seats reflect the share of votes; it was abolished in Northern Ireland in 1922 for local elections and in 1929 for Stormont.
